introduction: These readings concern places: the Shrines of Bahá’u’lláh and the Báb, the House in Baghdad, Mount Carmel and the Holy Land, the graves of believers. Some explain why a place is honoured, because a holy person walked there and the visitor is moved to remember; many are letters reporting that a pilgrim has arrived, prayed on someone's behalf, or must wait; others arrange the building of a tomb, the watering of a garden, the gift of a carpet or a lamp. Jacob at Bethel, the pilgrim psalms, the Qur’an's call to pilgrimage and Nehemiah among the ruins stand beside them. Jeremiah, Jesus, Peter, Seneca, Kabir, Milton and Emerson ask the questions holy places always raise: whether God is nearer there, what reverence may be shown to dust, and what a grave is for.
questions: The first readings say a place is revered for the sake of the person associated with it, and that lamps are lit for the visitors. What does that make of a holy place?
One reading says one may turn to the Shrine from anywhere, with no nearness or remoteness. Why then do people cross seas to reach it, and what do Seneca and Kabir say to them?
Peter raises Cornelius from his feet, and the readings confine prostration to a few places. Where is the line between reverence and worship of a place?
What do the many small letters, about arrivals, delays, carpets and gardens, show about how a community keeps its holy places?
Monica asked to be laid anywhere; Moses' grave is unknown. What are graves for?

outside.why: Exodus commands pure oil brought for the light of the tabernacle, to cause the lamp to burn always.
Joshua sets up stones so that children in time to come will ask what they mean, and be told.
Emerson complains that his age builds the sepulchres of the fathers and sees God through their eyes. When does honouring a site help a living faith, and when does it take its place?
Naaman, healed, asks to carry home two mules' burden of the land's earth on which to worship.
Moses is told to put off his shoes, for the place whereon he stands is holy ground.
Daniel in exile prays three times a day with his windows open toward Jerusalem.
Solomon asks that God hear the prayers his people make toward this place.
The psalm says of Zion: thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof.
Jacob wakes and says: surely the Lord is in this place, and I knew it not; this is the gate of heaven.
Haggai asks whether it is time to dwell in panelled houses while the house of God lies waste.
John records that there was a garden where Jesus was crucified, and in the garden a new sepulchre.
Jacob charges his sons to bury him with his fathers in the cave his family had bought.
The wise men, seeing the star stand, rejoice with exceeding great joy.
Lamentations mourns the city that sits solitary, that was full of people.
The exiles by the rivers of Babylon wept when they remembered Zion.
Cyrus king of Persia proclaims that he is charged to build a house at Jerusalem, and invites the people to go up.
Nehemiah shows his companions the city lying waste and says: come, let us build.
Jeremiah warns against trusting in the words, the temple of the Lord, the temple of the Lord. When does care for a holy house become trust in a building?
Isaiah says the Lord will comfort all the waste places of Zion.
The Qur’an says that but for God's defence, cloisters, churches, oratories and mosques would have been pulled down.
At Sinai bounds are set about the mount, and the people warned not to go up into it.
The psalmist would rather be a doorkeeper in the house of his God than dwell in the tents of wickedness.
Isaiah gives the excellency of Carmel and Sharon to the desert that shall rejoice and blossom.
The psalm says the Lord has chosen Zion and desired it for his habitation.
Elijah has all Israel gathered to him unto mount Carmel, the mountain the reading addresses.
The psalm calls the mountain of God's holiness beautiful for situation, the joy of the whole earth.
Luke says that Jesus went out into a mountain to pray, and continued all night in prayer.
The Light Verse is the source of the reading's figures of niche, lamp and light.
The Qur’an speaks of a far distant place of worship whose neighbourhood God has blessed.
Hebrews speaks of so great a cloud of witnesses compassing the faithful about.
Elijah, hidden by a brook, is fed by ravens morning and evening.
Shelley's traveller finds the wreck of a king's monument, and round it the lone and level sands.
The angels ask the women at the tomb: why seek ye the living among the dead? What does it say that for three hundred years no one looked for the grave?
John tells of Mary standing at the sepulchre weeping, and stooping to look in.
Abram is told to leave his country for a land that God will show him.
The psalmist wishes for wings like a dove, to fly away and be at rest.
The psalm says of the city: they shall prosper that love thee.
The Qur’an has Abraham proclaim the pilgrimage, and people come on foot and on every lean camel from every deep ravine.
The psalm blesses pilgrims in whose heart are the ways, who go from strength to strength.
The psalm says that they who go down to the sea in ships see the wonders of the Lord in the deep.
The pilgrim's psalm begins: I was glad when they said unto me, let us go into the house of the Lord.
Acts tells of an Ethiopian officer who had come to Jerusalem to worship and was returning in his chariot.
The Song of Songs says: I sat down under his shadow with great delight.
Isaiah foresees many people saying, come, let us go up to the mountain of the Lord.
The queen of Sheba, hearing of Solomon's fame, comes to Jerusalem to see for herself.
The psalm calls God a refuge and strength, a very present help in trouble.
The psalmist finds God wherever he might go, in heaven, in the grave, in the uttermost parts of the sea. Is refuge found in one Spot, or is the Spot a sign of what is everywhere?
Jesus tells Thomas: blessed are they that have not seen, and yet have believed.
When Cornelius falls at Peter's feet, Peter raises him: stand up, I myself also am a man. What keeps reverence at a threshold from becoming the worship of a place?
John falls at an angel's feet and is told: see thou do it not; worship God. Why might a faith confine prostration to a very few places?
Paul writes to friends he has not met: I long to see you.
The psalmist desires one thing: to dwell in the house of the Lord and behold his beauty.
Luke says the parents of Jesus went to Jerusalem every year at the feast.
The psalmist's soul longs, even faints, for the courts of the Lord.
Jesus tells his disciples to pray that their journey be not in the winter.
Jesus asks who would build a tower without first sitting down to count the cost.
Proverbs says that hope deferred makes the heart sick, but when the desire comes it is a tree of life.
Habakkuk is told: though it tarry, wait for it; it will surely come.
Proverbs says a man's heart devises his way, but the Lord directs his steps.
Hebrews says: be not forgetful to entertain strangers, for some have entertained angels unawares.
The Qur’an makes pilgrimage to the House a duty for whoever can find a way there.
Deuteronomy commands that three times in a year all shall appear before the Lord in the place he chooses.
Simeon, just and devout, waited in Jerusalem for the consolation of Israel, and it was revealed to him that he would see it.
The psalmist prays: send out thy light and thy truth; let them bring me unto thy holy hill.
Seneca says we need not beg a temple-keeper to let us near, for God is near you, with you, within you. Why then travel to a holy place?
Jesus says of a woman's devotion that her sins, which are many, are forgiven, for she loved much.
Matthew tells of wise men who came from the east to Jerusalem, asking where the child was.
Kabir has God say: I am beside thee, in neither temple nor mosque, neither Kaaba nor Kailash. What does a pilgrim find at the Spot that could not be found at home?
Jesus says of Mary, who stayed at his feet, that she has chosen the good part.
Isaiah has God promise to bring his people from the east and gather them from the west.
Hebrews says that Abraham, when called, went out not knowing whither he went.
Mark says that Jesus took the children up in his arms and blessed them.
The Ethiopian pilgrim, baptized on the road, went on his way rejoicing.
Paul says that though absent in the flesh he is present in spirit.
John writes: I have no greater joy than to hear that my children walk in truth.
Paul thanks God upon every remembrance of his friends, in every prayer.
Simon Peter falls down at Jesus' knees, saying: depart from me, for I am a sinful man.
Milton addresses a Spirit that prefers before all temples the upright heart and pure. What does a forehead pressed to holy dust add to an upright heart?
Paul lists his journeys: perils of waters, of robbers, in the wilderness, in the sea.
The psalm says: serve the Lord with gladness; come before his presence with singing.
Jesus rebukes those who build the tombs of the prophets and garnish their sepulchres while refusing what the prophets said. What makes the care of a grave more than ornament?
The Fathers say: let thy house be a house of meeting for the wise.
Deuteronomy says that no man knows the sepulchre of Moses unto this day. Why might a faith leave its greatest grave unmarked, and what is gained by marking one?
Pericles says that heroes have the whole earth for their tomb, and no single monument holds them.
The Preacher says there is a time to build up, and a time for every purpose.
Genesis gives the body its end in a sentence: dust thou art, and unto dust shalt thou return.
Stevenson asks for a grave under the wide and starry sky: here he lies where he longed to be.
George Eliot honours those who lived faithfully a hidden life and rest in unvisited tombs.
Monica told her sons to lay her body anywhere and only to remember her at the altar. Is a grave for the dead, or for the living who visit it?
Proverbs says that the memory of the just is blessed, as this grave is called blessed.
Luke says the disciples returned to Jerusalem with great joy and were continually in the temple.
Guru Gobind Singh says that the temple and the mosque are the same. Does reverence for one's own shrine teach reverence for another's?
Paul says: I have planted, Apollos watered, but God gave the increase.
Paul tells friends he is parted from them in presence, not in heart.
The pilgrim's psalm ends: the Lord shall preserve thy going out and thy coming in.
Bunyan begins his pilgrim's story: as I walked through the wilderness of this world.
Jesus says of the widow who gave two mites to the temple treasury that she gave more than all.
When a woman pours costly ointment on Jesus, some ask why this waste, since it might have been given to the poor. How are gifts for a shrine to be weighed against other needs?
Exodus says that every one whose heart stirred him up brought an offering for the work of the tabernacle.
The psalmist remembers God upon his bed and meditates on him in the night watches.

psalm-take-pleasure-in-her-stones.text: Thou shalt arise, and have mercy upon Zion: for the time to favour her, yea, the set time, is come. For thy servants take pleasure in her stones, and favour the dust thereof

exodus-every-one-whose-heart-stirred-him.text: And they came, every one whose heart stirred him up, and every one whom his spirit made willing, and they brought the Lord's offering to the work of the tabernacle of the congregation, and for all his service, and for the holy garments

mark-why-was-this-waste.text: And there were some that had indignation within themselves, and said, Why was this waste of the ointment made? For it might have been sold for more than three hundred pence, and have been given to the poor. And they murmured against her. And Jesus said, Let her alone; why trouble ye her? she hath wrought a good work on me

acts-stand-up-i-myself-also-am-a-man.text: And as Peter was coming in, Cornelius met him, and fell down at his feet, and worshipped him. But Peter took him up, saying, Stand up; I myself also am a man

john-in-the-garden-a-new-sepulchre.text: Now in the place where he was crucified there was a garden; and in the garden a new sepulchre, wherein was never man yet laid

exodus-lamp-to-burn-always.text: And thou shalt command the children of Israel, that they bring thee pure oil olive beaten for the light, to cause the lamp to burn always

genesis-bury-me-with-my-fathers.text: And he charged them, and said unto them, I am to be gathered unto my people: bury me with my fathers in the cave that is in the field of Ephron the Hittite
